questions.statement: Which sentence gives the main idea of the radio report?
questions.context: A radio station in Alajuela broadcasts a short report about a new bike lane.

options.text: The city is building a protected bike lane downtown.
options.feedback: Correct: the opening sentence states the topic itself, and the rest of the report only adds detail to it.

options.text: The report lasts two minutes.
options.feedback: The length of the report is a detail about the broadcast, not about what the report is saying.

options.text: Rush hour traffic downtown has grown.
options.feedback: Growing traffic is only one supporting fact, so it narrows the report down to a single point.

options.text: The lane will need repairs in five years.
options.feedback: Future repairs are a detail that fits inside the bigger news about the new lane.

questions.explanation:
The main idea is the one general message that the whole piece supports; numbers, times and examples only illustrate it.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase tells you the speaker is stating the main point?
questions.context: A host in Heredia interviews a coffee grower from Tarrazu on the radio.

options.text: Interestingly enough
options.feedback: Interestingly adds colour to an aside; it introduces something extra, not the central message.

options.text: On the other hand
options.feedback: On the other hand marks a contrast with an earlier point, so it signals a second idea instead.

options.text: The main reason is that
options.feedback: Correct: this phrase is an explicit signpost that tells the listener the core of the talk begins here.

options.text: By the way
options.feedback: By the way marks an aside or a change of subject, so it moves away from the main point.

questions.explanation:
Speakers mark structure with phrases: mainly, the point is or to sum up announce the central idea, while however and by the way introduce side points.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the topic sentence of her lecture?
questions.context: A professor in San Jose lectures her class about traffic in the capital.

options.text: The lecture lasts fifty minutes, so take notes carefully.
options.feedback: This is an instruction about the class, so it belongs to the situation, not to the subject.

options.text: Traffic in San Jose grows because more people drive instead of taking the bus.
options.feedback: Correct: it names the general subject and its reason, so every later detail in the talk supports it.

options.text: Some drivers leave the car at home on Tuesdays.
options.feedback: One group habit on one weekday is a single example, so it supports the topic without stating it.

options.text: The blue chart on the screen shows data from 2019.
options.feedback: Saying which chart appears describes the visuals, not the message the lecture delivers.

questions.explanation:
The topic sentence states the subject in general terms; the sentences after it offer facts, figures and examples that only explain it.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the main purpose of that radio spot?
questions.context: A station in Alajuela airs a thirty second spot for a play at the Teatro Nacional.

options.text: Explain the full plot of the play for its audience.
options.feedback: A plot summary belongs to a review; this short spot gives no details about the story.

options.text: Report how many people attended last night.
options.feedback: Attendance figures report the past, while a promotion is about what listeners can still do.

options.text: Compare ticket prices with another theatre in San Jose.
options.feedback: No rival theatre appears in the spot, so no comparison of prices is ever made.

options.text: Tell listeners where and when to get their tickets.
options.feedback: Correct: the mention of the door and the show times are the facts a listener needs in order to act.

questions.explanation:
Short spots have one clear aim. Ask what the listener is meant to do or learn, and that question reveals the main purpose.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which summary keeps the main idea of her notes?
questions.context: A student in Guanacaste took notes on a talk about turtle protection in Playa Grande.

options.text: Playa Grande protects sea turtles by limiting lights and nesting zones.
options.feedback: Correct: it keeps the topic and its one purpose, dropping the numbers and logistics that only supported it.

options.text: The talk was on Thursday in room four with about sixty students.
options.feedback: The day, the room and the head count are details about the talk, not about its message.

options.text: One ranger counted forty nests in July and thirty in August.
options.feedback: Nest counts are the evidence inside the talk, so they support the summary instead of being it.

options.text: Students asked two questions about plastic waste at the end.
options.feedback: Audience questions and one example of waste are side moments, not the central claim.

questions.explanation:
A summary keeps the general message and drops narrow facts such as numbers, rooms and small events, so it ends shorter than the text.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is wrong with Sofia's summary of the bus talk?
questions.context: Sofia in Heredia wrote a summary of a talk about public transport that is too narrow.

options.text: It uses the past tense instead of the present simple.
options.feedback: Tense is not the problem; the sentence is grammatically fine and the fault lies in the content.

options.text: It gives one timetable detail, not the main argument of the talk.
options.feedback: Correct: a summary must carry the central claim, and a single timetable fact cannot stand for the talk.

options.text: It repeats the name of the bus company too many times.
options.feedback: The company name appears only once, so repetition is not what weakens this summary.

options.text: It is too long for the space allowed on the exam form.
options.feedback: The summary is short, so length is not the problem here; choosing the right idea is.

questions.explanation:
A summary fails when it keeps only a detail that stood out. Ask whether your sentence could describe the whole piece or just one moment.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which order of sections does this talk most likely follow?
questions.context: A radio talk in Puntarenas about the new port is given as problem, cause and solution.

options.text: Problem, solution, cause
options.feedback: This reaches the answer before giving the reason, so the listener meets the solution too early.

options.text: Cause, solution, problem
options.feedback: A cause cannot be explained before the problem that produced it, so this order runs backwards.

options.text: Solution, problem, cause
options.feedback: Starting with the solution and ending with the problem inverts the natural build of a talk.

options.text: Problem, cause, solution
options.feedback: Correct: expository talks usually state the problem, then its cause, and only then the solution.

questions.explanation:
Expository talks follow a predictable order: problem, then cause, then solution. Tracking it helps you recall the main ideas.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The coach says, "We lose matches in the last minutes." What is the implied idea?
questions.context: A coach in Desamparados talks to his players before a tournament in Quepos.

options.text: The team must improve its fitness and focus at the end of games.
options.feedback: Correct: the complaint points to late match weakness, so the implied message is what must change.

options.text: The team lost every match in the tournament.
options.feedback: The remark never claims that every match was lost, so this summary overstates what was said.

options.text: The coach wants a larger field for the final match.
options.feedback: The size of the field is never mentioned, so that conclusion is invented rather than implied.

options.text: Training starts earlier than the team expected.
options.feedback: No training schedule comes up in the remark, so this idea has no support in what was said.

questions.explanation:
Speakers often imply the main idea instead of stating it; the complaint about the last minutes points to what must improve.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She says, "Well, I suppose the law might possibly help." What is her attitude?
questions.context: A reporter in San Jose asks a farmer in Grecia about a new law on water use.

options.text: She fully supports the law and expects large results.
options.feedback: Hedges like might possibly rule out the full confidence and the big results this option claims.

options.text: She is angry and ready to ignore the law.
options.feedback: Nothing in the hedging shows anger, which would need sharper and more loaded wording.

options.text: She is politely doubtful and not fully convinced.
options.feedback: Correct: well and I suppose are hedges that signal polite doubt rather than open support.

options.text: She has not understood the reporter's question.
options.feedback: Her answer is clearly on the topic, so the hesitation comes from her opinion, not confusion.

questions.explanation:
Hedges such as I suppose, maybe and a little soften a claim, so heavy hedging signals doubt while flat wording signals confidence.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which summary best represents the whole interview?
questions.context: A university station in Alajuela interviews two people about bicycles in the city.

options.text: Both guests asked for more bike lanes in San Jose.
options.feedback: This keeps only the shared request and drops the disagreement, which is a main part of the interview.

options.text: The guests explain why bicycles matter, then disagree on who should pay for new lanes.
options.feedback: Correct: it gives the shared topic and the central clash, so it covers what the interview is about.

options.text: The host asked about the price of bicycle helmets downtown.
options.feedback: A single question about helmets is a minor moment and says nothing about the overall content.

options.text: The interview was recorded on a windy afternoon downtown.
options.feedback: Recording conditions sit outside the content of the interview and cannot be its main idea.

questions.explanation:
A summary of an interview must cover the shared topic and any disagreement that shapes it; omitting the clash hides half of the idea.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The speaker says the problem is not cost. What was the main idea?
questions.context: During a listening test, a student in Cartago writes down a wrong summary.

options.text: Cost is the real problem of the project.
options.feedback: The opening denies exactly that link, so this summary reverses the speaker's contrast.

options.text: Nothing in the talk is connected with cost.
options.feedback: Cost is mentioned and then set aside, so a summary that drops it loses the point of the contrast.

options.text: The real problem of the project is something other than cost.
options.feedback: Correct: not cost tells the listener the speaker is replacing one idea with a different one.

options.text: Cost is the only problem the project has.
options.feedback: This contradicts the claim that the problem is not cost, which rules cost out instead of confirming it.

questions.explanation:
Contrastive openings flag the main idea: despite, in fact and not X but Y tell you the speaker is replacing one idea with another.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which host phrase signals that a new main section is starting?
questions.context: A podcast recorded in Heredia has three sections and the host names each one.

options.text: Now, the second part of the story...
options.feedback: Correct: the second part is an explicit signpost that a new main section of the show has begun.

options.text: You know, it was really something.
options.feedback: This is a personal reaction to what was already said, so it comments instead of opening a section.

options.text: Kind of a big deal, honestly.
options.feedback: An informal comment about size carries no signal about a move to another part of the talk.

options.text: I mean, basically, whatever.
options.feedback: Fillers like I mean and basically hide the speaker's place in the talk rather than showing it.

questions.explanation:
Structural signposts include first, next, finally and the main reason; fillers like you know carry no information about the shape.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which answer style suits a question about the report's main idea?
questions.context: At a school in Puntarenas students practise a listening test with a radio report.

options.text: It repeats the exact numbers the reporter read out twice.
options.feedback: Figures are details; a main idea answer has to hold for the whole report, not for one number.

options.text: It gives the reporter's opinion about the people he quotes.
options.feedback: The reporter's own view is a side comment, while the main idea is what the report supports.

options.text: It lists every place and date mentioned in the report.
options.feedback: A list of places and dates describes the content in detail but never says what it is about.

options.text: It states the general point that the whole report supports.
options.feedback: Correct: a main idea answer covers the whole piece and can be proved with evidence from several parts.

questions.explanation:
Detail answers repeat one narrow fact; main idea answers generalise, so they must be true for every part of the piece.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Her summary says only "Water is important". How can she improve it?
questions.context: A student in Puntarenas wrote a summary that was far too general after a talk in Limon.

options.text: By adding more opinion about why water matters to her.
options.feedback: Personal opinion adds a voice the talk never used and still leaves the content vague.

options.text: By naming what the talk said about water use and what followed from it.
options.feedback: Correct: a main idea names the specific subject and its consequence, not only the general truth.

options.text: By dropping every detail she heard in the recording.
options.feedback: Summaries still need content; removing all the detail leaves nothing for a reader to understand.

options.text: By copying the first sentence the speaker said.
options.feedback: Copying the opening works only when that sentence states the topic, which here it does not.

questions.explanation:
An over general summary is fixed by naming the specific subject and the point made about it, not by adding opinions.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which headline states the main idea of the whole bulletin?
questions.context: A news bulletin in Escazu reports a road project and interviews two residents.

options.text: A resident says the dust is hard to avoid.
options.feedback: The dust complaint is one resident's view, so it cannot stand as the headline for the whole item.

options.text: Bus drivers want the old route kept for a year.
options.feedback: The drivers' request is a side detail, while the road itself is what the bulletin is mainly about.

options.text: A new road will replace the old bridge over the Rio Torres.
options.feedback: Correct: it names the single event the report explains, and the rest of the item supports it.

options.text: The project begins after the heavy rains in November.
options.feedback: The start date is a scheduling detail that fits inside the bigger story about the new road.

questions.explanation:
A headline must cover every part of the report; test it by asking whether the interviews and figures still fit under it.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which signposted part carries the main idea of the debate?
questions.context: A radio debate in Cartago is split into three signposted parts by the host.

options.text: The closing response, because it comes last.
options.feedback: Coming last does not make a part central; a response usually reacts to the argument already made.

options.text: The opening history, because it comes first.
options.feedback: The history sets the scene, so it frames the debate without carrying its central point.

options.text: The longest section, because it takes more time.
options.feedback: Length measures time, not importance, so the longest section is not automatically the main one.

options.text: The main argument, because the other two parts serve it.
options.feedback: Correct: the opening sets up the argument and the closing answers it, so the argument is central.

questions.explanation:
When a talk is split into parts, the central one is the part the others serve: the opening frames it and the closing reacts to it.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which line is only a detail of the show, not its main idea?
questions.context: A radio show in Liberia talks about a new library in Guanacaste.

options.text: Local reading habits need a real push.
options.feedback: This line generalises the whole item, so it works as the main idea the show supports.

options.text: The library opens its shelves with four hundred books.
options.feedback: Correct: a number of books is one concrete fact inside the item, not the message behind the report.

options.text: Students can use free internet inside the building.
options.feedback: Free internet is a real service in the item, but it is only one point among several details.

options.text: The programme finishes at ten o'clock tonight.
options.feedback: The end time belongs to the broadcast schedule, not to the content the show is about.

questions.explanation:
Details are specific facts such as numbers, services and times; the main idea turns them into one message a listener can repeat.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The student writes "Buses should be free." Whose view is that?
questions.context: A reporter in Alajuela questions a farmer about buses in the canton.

options.text: The reporter's, because he asked the question.
options.feedback: Asking a question does not mean holding a view; the reporter is asking, not claiming.

options.text: Nobody's, because the claim appears twice.
options.feedback: How often a claim is repeated says nothing about which voice it belongs to in the recording.

options.text: The guest's, because only the guest argued for it.
options.feedback: Correct: the reporter frames the talk with questions while the guest carries the opinion.

options.text: The listener's, because the speaker sounds persuasive.
options.feedback: Tone shows the speaker's manner, not the listener's opinion, so this attribution has no basis.

questions.explanation:
In an interview the main idea usually belongs to the guest, while the host only frames it, so track the voices as you listen.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The host says: "Today we look at how three schools cut waste." What is the topic?
questions.context: A podcast recorded in Cartago opens with a short introduction by its host.

options.text: How schools reduce the waste they produce.
options.feedback: Correct: the opening names the topic, and the whole episode goes on to explain that one subject.

options.text: The schools failed to manage their rubbish.
options.feedback: Failure would need words like failed or could not, which the introduction never uses.

options.text: The podcast will interview three waste companies.
options.feedback: The number three modifies schools, not companies, so no interview with businesses is promised.

options.text: Waste rose in Cartago during the last school term.
options.feedback: A rise in waste is one point inside the episode, not something the introduction announces.

questions.explanation:
An opening line states the topic: today we look at plus a noun phrase gives the main idea before any detail begins.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which one sentence summary would serve a reader who missed the report?
questions.context: A student in Escazu must summarise a three minute report for a classmate who missed it.

options.text: The speaker argued that farms should stop using plastic bags.
options.feedback: Naming only farms and plastic bags leaves out the wider problem and the response the report covers.

options.text: The talk closed with a joke about coffee prices in Tarrazu.
options.feedback: A closing joke is a feature of the delivery, not the substance a reader who missed it needs.

options.text: The report repeated three statistics about crop yields last year.
options.feedback: Repeated figures are the support the report rests on, so they cannot replace the point itself.

options.text: The report explained why food waste rose and what cities can do about it.
options.feedback: Correct: it names both the problem and the response, so an absent reader still gets the whole story.

questions.explanation:
A summary for an absent reader must cover the problem and the response in one sentence, so the logic of the item survives.
